name: seanmonstar/reqwest
description: Evaluation questions for reqwest, a higher-level Rust HTTP client library wrapping hyper. Held-out Rust corpus written from reading the real source in eval_repos/reqwest, independent of RepoGuide's Rust semantic provider implementation -- not tuned against provider output.

questions.question: What are reqwest's core async types and how do they relate to each other?
questions.expectedAnswer: `Client` (holding a shared `Arc<ClientRef>` of pooled connection state) is created via `ClientBuilder`, itself created via `Client::builder()` or `ClientBuilder::new()`. Calling a method like `Client::get()` returns a `RequestBuilder`, which builds and sends a `Request`, ultimately producing a `Response`. All four live in `src/async_impl/`, re-exported at the crate root.

questions.question: How does reqwest express "this type converts into a Body" for something like a plain String, using Rust's `impl Trait for Type` syntax?
questions.expectedAnswer: Via `impl From<String> for Body` in `src/async_impl/body.rs` -- one of several `From<T> for Body` impls in that same file (also covering `Bytes`, `Vec<u8>`, `&'static [u8]`, `&'static str`, `File`, and `hyper::Body`). This is reqwest's idiomatic way of supporting `Body::from(...)`/`.into()` conversions from many source types, all declared as separate, unambiguous trait impls rather than one generic conversion function.

questions.question: Is reqwest one flat module, or does it split its sync and async APIs into separate module trees?
questions.expectedAnswer: It's split three ways, gated by cfg/feature flags in `src/lib.rs` via the `if_hyper!`/`if_wasm!` macros: `async_impl` (the default hyper-based async API -- `Client`, `Body`, `Request`, `Response`, etc.), `blocking` (a synchronous wrapper, only compiled with the `blocking` feature), and `wasm` (a separate implementation for `wasm32` targets). Only one of `async_impl`/`wasm` is compiled for a given target; `blocking` is additive on top of `async_impl`.

questions.question: Where is the Client struct defined?
Which file declares the redirect Policy struct?
Where is the IntoUrl trait declared, and what supertrait bound does it carry?
questions.expectedAnswer: In `src/into_url.rs`, line 7: `pub trait IntoUrl: IntoUrlSealed {}` -- it requires (extends) the private `IntoUrlSealed` trait, which is reqwest's "sealed trait" pattern: only types within the reqwest crate can implement `IntoUrlSealed`, so external crates can't implement `IntoUrl` themselves.

questions.question: Where is reqwest's Error type declared, and what's the name of its Result type alias?
questions.expectedAnswer: `Error` is declared in `src/error.rs`, line 20; the alias is `pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, Error>;` at line 13 of the same file.

questions.question: Where is the ClientBuilder::build method that finally constructs a real Client?
questions.expectedAnswer: In `src/async_impl/client.rs`, line 407, inside a second `impl ClientBuilder` block (there's an earlier one starting at line 278 for `ClientBuilder::new` and its configuration methods).

questions.question: Trace what happens when you call the package-level reqwest::get() function.
questions.expectedAnswer: `get()` (in `src/lib.rs`) calls `Client::builder().build()?.get(url).send().await` in one chained expression: `Client::builder()` returns a fresh `ClientBuilder`, `.build()` turns it into a real `Client` (or propagates a build error), `.get(url)` returns a `RequestBuilder`, and `.send().await` executes it into a `Response`. Its doc comment explicitly warns this creates a brand-new internal `Client` on every call, so it shouldn't be used for repeated requests.

expectedFlow.description: Module-level convenience function chaining builder construction, build, and request-send into one call.

questions.question: What does Client::new() do internally?
questions.expectedAnswer: It calls `ClientBuilder::new().build().expect("Client::new()")` -- i.e. it delegates to the exact same builder path as `Client::builder()`, but panics (via `.expect`) instead of returning a `Result` if construction fails (e.g. if the TLS backend can't initialize). Its own doc comment tells callers to use `Client::builder()` instead if they want to handle that failure as an `Error`.

expectedFlow.description: Panicking convenience constructor delegating to the same builder path as the fallible Client::builder().

questions.question: What does Client::builder() actually do?
questions.expectedAnswer: Almost nothing on its own -- its whole body is `ClientBuilder::new()`. Its doc comment says as much: "This is the same as `ClientBuilder::new()`." It exists purely as a more discoverable entry point named after the type it produces.

expectedFlow.description: One-line associated function delegating directly to another type's own constructor.

questions.question: How does a reqwest Response get converted into a Body, and where does that conversion live relative to Body's own declaration?
questions.expectedAnswer: Via `impl From<Response> for Body` in `src/async_impl/response.rs`, whose `from` method calls `Body::wrap(r.res.into_body())`. This is notable because `Body` itself is declared in a *different* file, `src/async_impl/body.rs` -- one of the rare real cases where an impl block for a given type lives outside the file that declares the type (confirmed empirically: only 2 of 108 impl'd types in this crate are split this way).

expectedFlow.description: Cross-file trait impl converting one async_impl type into another, declared away from the target type's own file.

questions.question: Explain reqwest::get, step by step.
questions.expectedAnswer: It's an `async fn` generic over `T: IntoUrl`. Its entire body is one chained expression: build a default `Client` via `Client::builder().build()?`, immediately call `.get(url)` on it to get a `RequestBuilder`, then `.send().await` to execute the request and get a `Response` (or propagate any error via `?`). No client is reused across calls -- a new one is constructed every time, exactly as its doc comment warns.

questions.question: Walk through IntoUrlSealed::into_url for a plain Url -- what does it actually check?
questions.expectedAnswer: On non-wasm targets it just checks `self.has_host()`: if the URL has a host, it's returned as-is (`Ok(self)`); otherwise it returns a `url_bad_scheme` error. On `wasm32` targets there's an extra carve-out first: if the scheme is `blob` and the remainder of the URL (after stripping `blob:`) parses as a valid URL itself, the original blob URL is accepted early, since `has_host()` is always false for blob URLs and would otherwise incorrectly reject them.

questions.question: What does the Policy struct's doc comment tell you about reqwest's default redirect behavior, and what are the three ways to construct one?
questions.expectedAnswer: The doc comment says the default policy catches redirect loops and follows a maximum of 10 redirects before erroring. Three constructors exist: `Policy::limited(max)` (same loop-catching behavior, but a caller-chosen max hop count instead of 10), `Policy::none()` (disables all redirect-following), and a `custom` variant built from a caller-supplied function -- for which the doc comment explicitly warns that loop protection isn't automatic and must be implemented by the custom function itself.

questions.question: Where does reqwest implement a GraphQL query builder?
questions.expectedAnswer: It doesn't -- reqwest is a general-purpose HTTP client; it has no GraphQL-specific query construction, schema handling, or execution anywhere in its source.

questions.question: Does reqwest include its own HTML parser or DOM implementation for scraping response bodies?
questions.expectedAnswer: No. reqwest only handles the HTTP transport layer and generic body serialization/deserialization (e.g. JSON via serde); parsing HTML or building a DOM is entirely outside its scope and isn't implemented anywhere in the crate.

questions.question: Does reqwest implement its own TLS handshake or cryptographic primitives from scratch?
questions.expectedAnswer: No -- reqwest delegates TLS entirely to existing backend crates (native-tls or rustls, selected via Cargo feature flags such as `default-tls`/`rustls-tls`), configured through `src/tls.rs`. It doesn't implement any cryptography or handshake logic of its own.

questions.question: I just edited src/async_impl/client.rs locally but haven't reindexed. Which structs does it define, and could the index be stale for them?
questions.expectedAnswer: It defines `Client` (line 93) and `ClientBuilder` (line 99), among other private types like `Config` and `ClientRef`. Since the file was just modified without reindexing, any cached understanding of it -- including this answer -- may be stale and should be re-verified against the current file contents.
